Round 1 · 6 possible points

The Missing Left Side

Spatial attention

Daniel
After a right-sided stroke, Daniel began leaving the left side of his paintings blank. He could still see to his left on a visual-field test. His scan showed damage to the right insula and putamen. Later, he painted across the canvas, but the two sides still differed.

Clue: Find the lateral sulcus on slides 6–7 and P (putamen) in the legend on slide 8.

Round 2 · 6 possible points

A Small Tract, a Large Memory Problem

Memory pathways

Ravi
Ravi could remember older events but struggled to recall what he had just been told or what he had eaten for breakfast. His MRI showed stroke damage to the fornix on both sides.

Clue: Compare the fornix on slide 32 (PDF p. 26) with the corpus callosum on slide 11, panel C.

Round 3 · 5 possible points

The Drooping Eyelid and Dilated Pupil

Eye movements and blood vessels

Mei
Mei began seeing double. Her right eyelid drooped, and her right pupil was larger than the left. A scan of her blood vessels showed a bulge (an aneurysm) in the right posterior communicating artery, close to a nerve that moves the eye.

Clue: Find the artery on slide 14. A bulging blood vessel can press on a nearby nerve.

Cortical landmarks and basal ganglia
Cranial nerves (optional)

CN II carries visual input. CN III supplies most eye muscles, elevates the upper eyelid and carries pupil-constricting parasympathetic fibres. CN IV supplies superior oblique; CN VI supplies lateral rectus.

CN III motor neurons and the preganglionic Edinger–Westphal parasympathetic neurons lie in the midbrain. Trace parasympathetic fibres through CN III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae. CN III runs near the posterior communicating artery.

        Blood supply and stroke (optional)

        Unscored practice · Slides 13–16 and 30.

        Stroke example: connect the lesion, function and blood supply

        A scan shows an infarct in the right primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus. Which combination best fits this lesion?

        DistributionAnatomical contextReasoning implication
        ACAMainly medial frontal and parietalConsider leg representation and initiation systems
        MCAMuch lateral cortex and deep branchesLanguage, attention and motor effects depend on side and branch
        PCAMuch occipital and inferomedial temporal tissue; deep branchesVisual and memory effects depend on involved structures
        PerforatorsDeep nuclei and white matterA strategic lesion may disrupt a large network
        Border zonesBetween major territoriesConsider perfusion and lesion distribution
        Arterial routes, collateral links and venous drainage

        Internal carotids give rise to ACA and MCA. Vertebral arteries unite as basilar, which usually ends in PCAs. Communicating arteries provide potential collateral routes, with anatomical variation. The MCA is not a segment of the circle of Willis. Veins drain through dural sinuses towards internal jugular veins, following a different organisation from arterial territories.
